title: Forest plots: align estimates, intervals and the no-effect value
summary: Compare like-for-like effects on one scale and explain what each interval and marker means.
body:
Compare like-for-like effects on one scale and explain what each interval and marker means.

Choose one effect measure

A forest plot places estimates on a shared horizontal scale with an interval beside each estimate. Mean differences, risk ratios and odds ratios cannot be mixed as though their numbers shared a unit. State the effect measure, population, comparison direction and interval method before plotting. The no-effect value is zero for an additive difference and one for a multiplicative ratio. A log-scaled ratio axis often makes equal proportional changes on either side of one visually comparable; it cannot accept zero or negative endpoints. Signed differences have a different zero reference and should not inherit ratio-axis labels.

Keep the interval type attached

A horizontal line may be a confidence interval, a credible interval, a sensitivity range or something else. Say which. Do not infer that a row with an interval touching the no-effect line is equivalent to a row with a wide interval far beyond it. Both estimate magnitude and precision matter. Asymmetric error bars explain why endpoints must be kept as numbers, not reconstructed from a visual radius. When an interval exceeds the plot boundary, use a clipped-end marker and print its true endpoint. Never replace the endpoint with the axis maximum in the underlying data.

Marker area needs a contract

A larger square can indicate greater analytic weight, sample size or merely visual emphasis. Those are not interchangeable. If marker area represents a weight, name the weighting method and provide the numeric weights. A pooled estimate at the bottom is a separate calculation, not the average of x positions on the screen; omit it when the included rows are not meaningfully combinable. Area-scaled symbols follow the same rule: doubling a marker radius quadruples its area. A plain point estimate with equal marker size is safer when weights are not part of the analysis.

Sort without changing meaning

Sorting rows by effect size can make a striking ladder but may hide prespecified groups or study chronology. Declare the row order, retain stable IDs, and distinguish subgroups without implying that adjacency is evidence of similarity. A plot of model variants should note which intervals are correlated because they share data; counting each variant as an independent result overstates evidence. Uncertainty and sample-size displays help explain sparse rows. Supply an accessible table with row ID, estimate, lower and upper bounds, unit, interval type and weight, then compare the chart against that table before publishing.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite, log

def ratio_forest_positions(
    rows: list[tuple[str, float, float, float]]
) -> list[tuple[str, float, float, float]]:
    names = [name for name, _, _, _ in rows]
    if len(names) != len(set(names)) or any(not name for name in names):
        raise ValueError("row names must be unique and nonempty")
    output = []
    for name, estimate, lower, upper in rows:
        if not all(isfinite(value) and value > 0
                   for value in (estimate, lower, upper)):
            raise ValueError("ratio estimates and endpoints must be positive")
        if not lower <= estimate <= upper:
            raise ValueError("estimate must lie within its interval")
        output.append((name, log(estimate), log(lower), log(upper)))
    return output

depot_comparisons = ratio_forest_positions([
    ("north depot", 1.25, 1.06, 1.47),
    ("south depot", 0.80, 0.65, 1.03),
])
assert depot_comparisons[0][1] > 0
assert depot_comparisons[1][1] < 0
assert log(1) == 0

Performance and operating cost

Validating and transforming N rows takes O(N) time and O(N) output space. The code prepares positive ratio estimates for a log axis; it does not calculate intervals, pool rows or assign weights. Keep original ratio values in the export because logarithmic positions are drawing coordinates. If a row has a zero, negative or undefined ratio, investigate the estimator rather than forcing it onto the log plot.

Common Mistakes

  • Mixing additive differences and ratios on one unlabeled axis.
  • Drawing the no-effect line at zero for a raw ratio plot.
  • Using square size as weight without stating the weighting rule.
  • Silently truncating interval endpoints or treating related model variants as independent studies.

Validation drill

Compare 47 depot-level rate ratios with intervals. Identify rows that need clipped-end markers, then explain why a pooled diamond should not be drawn until the estimands and weights are reviewed.

  • Diverging bars: put signed differences on one shared zero
  • Proportional-symbol maps: size circles by area, not radius
  • Uncertainty on charts: show denominators and intervals beside estimates

title: Scatterplot matrices: disclose which rows support each pair
summary: Treat pairwise missingness, scales and the number of comparisons as part of the matrix.
body:
Treat pairwise missingness, scales and the number of comparisons as part of the matrix.

Each cell has its own population

A scatterplot matrix shows pairwise relationships among several variables. If missing values differ by column, the cell for queue depth versus delay may use different records from the cell for delay versus cost. A common complete-case filter makes populations consistent but may discard many rows. Pairwise deletion retains more data but changes the population from cell to cell. State which policy was used and print the valid count in every cell. Correlation heatmaps face the same coverage problem but hide the underlying point clouds.

Use one variable scale across its row and column

A variable appearing on several axes should keep a common unit and domain where possible. Otherwise the apparent slope and spread change as a reader moves across the grid. Label only the outer axes if the layout is tight, but keep units available in a companion table. Transformations such as logarithms must be consistent for every appearance of the variable, and invalid nonpositive values need an explicit exclusion count. Log-scale boundaries should be chosen for the data, not merely to make a diagonal cluster look tidy.

A matrix multiplies visual tests

With seven variables there are 21 distinct off-diagonal pairs. One remarkable-looking cell may occur by chance, especially after inspecting many matrices, filters and periods. Use the display to generate questions rather than to announce discovered laws. Annotate pre-specified comparisons, and follow up with a model or analysis suited to the decision. Regression overlays need their own fit population and assumptions; a line in every cell can overwhelm the matrix and invite unsupported causal readings.

Control density and reading order

Plotting the same large cohort in 42 mirrored cells can be expensive and visually opaque. Use the lower triangle for points and reserve the diagonal for univariate distributions or compact count summaries. Sample only with a declared rule, preserving rare groups if that is part of the question. Overplotting techniques can reveal concentration without creating false individual positions. Sort variables in a stable, meaningful sequence and offer a per-cell data table or drill-down so the matrix remains usable at phone width and high zoom.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def pairwise_points(records: list[dict[str, float | None]],
                    horizontal: str, vertical: str
                   ) -> list[tuple[float, float]]:
    if not horizontal or not vertical or horizontal == vertical:
        raise ValueError("two distinct variable names required")
    points = []
    for record in records:
        x_value, y_value = record.get(horizontal), record.get(vertical)
        if x_value is None or y_value is None:
            continue
        if not isfinite(x_value) or not isfinite(y_value):
            raise ValueError("non-finite values require an explicit policy")
        points.append((x_value, y_value))
    return points

depot_rows = [
    {"queue": 47.0, "delay": 31.0, "cost": 81.0},
    {"queue": 59.0, "delay": None, "cost": 97.0},
    {"queue": 83.0, "delay": 43.0, "cost": None},
]
assert pairwise_points(depot_rows, "queue", "delay") == [(47, 31), (83, 43)]
assert pairwise_points(depot_rows, "queue", "cost") == [(47, 81), (59, 97)]

Performance and operating cost

For P variables and N records, preparing every unique pair costs O(P squared times N) time. Retaining all displayed points for the lower triangle can take O(P squared times N) space; stream or aggregate when that footprint is too large. The example uses pairwise deletion and makes no correlation or significance claim. Report the per-cell count and dropped-row policy so two adjacent clouds are not mistaken for identical cohorts.

Common Mistakes

  • Reporting one global sample size when cells use different valid rows.
  • Auto-scaling the same variable differently across matrix cells.
  • Treating the most striking of many inspected pairs as confirmed evidence.
  • Rendering mirrored dense cells without a detail view or sampling record.

Validation drill

Build a lower-triangle matrix for seven operational measures. Put valid-row counts in all 21 cells, fix each variable's scale across appearances and identify three relationships chosen before viewing the grid.

title: Streamgraphs: preserve totals behind a moving baseline
summary: Use a centered stack for shape exploration, but give readers a separate way to inspect the total.
body:
Use a centered stack for shape exploration, but give readers a separate way to inspect the total.

The baseline is a layout choice

A streamgraph stacks nonnegative category values over time around a moving or centered baseline. Its flowing shape can help reveal broad category shifts, but the vertical position of a layer is partly an artifact of the baseline calculation. Layer thickness represents value; the upper edge alone does not. Do not label the vertical axis like an ordinary zero-based stacked area chart unless it actually has a fixed zero. Stacked composition explains why categories and their denominator must be stable enough to compare.

Totals still need a view

Centering a total of 47 and a total of 188 both around the same midpoint can make the chart attractive while hiding the operational difference. Include a separate total line, a compact table or a conventional zero-based stacked view when volume matters. A streamgraph is a poor sole view for audit questions such as whether all categories reconcile to the source total. Waterfall reconciliation handles additive changes with a more explicit baseline. For each time bin, validate that layer values sum to the reported total before calculating any layout offset.

Order controls readability

A layer buried in the middle may be easier to follow than one whose boundaries both move erratically, but changing the order between frames makes categories impossible to track. Select a stable order and color identity for the whole time range. If categories enter or leave, distinguish true zero from missing data; an absent category record should not silently become a zero-thickness layer. Missing periods and provisional bins require an explicit display state, even in a decorative-looking flow chart.

Keep the raw table accessible

Layer thickness is hard to read precisely, particularly on a narrow viewport. Provide a table with period, category, value, total and any excluded share. Label categories directly where possible and offer keyboard-accessible inspection for the rest. Interactive chart access should preserve each period and category ID when focus moves. Export the stacking order and baseline algorithm so an updated chart library cannot silently change the shape while the underlying observations stay fixed.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def centered_stack(categories: list[str],
                   periods: list[dict[str, float]]
                  ) -> list[dict[str, tuple[float, float]]]:
    if not categories or len(categories) != len(set(categories)):
        raise ValueError("ordered categories must be unique")
    output = []
    for period in periods:
        if set(period) != set(categories):
            raise ValueError("each period needs every category, including real zeros")
        if any(not isfinite(value) or value < 0 for value in period.values()):
            raise ValueError("values must be finite and nonnegative")
        baseline = -sum(period.values()) / 2
        layers = {}
        for category in categories:
            upper = baseline + period[category]
            layers[category] = (baseline, upper)
            baseline = upper
        output.append(layers)
    return output

service_mix = centered_stack(
    ["routine", "urgent"],
    [{"routine": 47, "urgent": 59}, {"routine": 81, "urgent": 97}],
)
assert service_mix[0] == {
    "routine": (-53.0, -6.0), "urgent": (-6.0, 53.0)
}
assert service_mix[1]["urgent"][1] == 89.0

Performance and operating cost

For T periods and C categories, validation and centered stacking take O(TC) time and O(TC) output space. This code uses a simple centered baseline, not an optimized wiggle offset; those two layouts differ. It requires a complete category set per period and rejects negative measures. Keep the original values and totals for accessibility and reconciliation. For large C, crowded labels and thin layers may make small multiples or a ranked table clearer.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading the moving layer boundary as a zero-based value.
  • Using a centered streamgraph alone when the decision depends on total volume.
  • Changing category order across periods and making colors switch identity.
  • Replacing missing category records with zero without a recorded rule.

Validation drill

Show 47 reporting periods and eight service classes. Reconcile each total, hold category order fixed and place a separate total-volume line beside the centered streamgraph.

title: Horizon charts: trade vertical space for a harder value lookup
summary: Explain the baseline, band width and color order so compact time series remain decodable.
body:
Explain the baseline, band width and color order so compact time series remain decodable.

Folded bands need a key

A horizon chart divides a value's distance from a baseline into bands and overlays those bands in a short row. It can fit many series in little vertical space, but a reader must decode band color as well as vertical shape. State the baseline and numeric size of one band. If the chart shows deviations from 47 incidents per day, a value of 87 occupies two 20-unit bands above that reference, not 87 units of vertical height. Baseline integrity matters more when the display has been folded.

Positive and negative need separate meaning

For signed deviations, use distinguishable sequences for above and below the baseline, not just a lighter and darker tint of one hue. Include text labels for the sign and a small decoding key with concrete values. A monochrome or color-vision test should still allow readers to distinguish the two directions through texture, labels or a paired table. Accessible color alternatives are a requirement of the underlying comparison, not a finishing layer. Missing observations need a gap; they are not zero deviation.

Fix a common band domain

If each row chooses its own band width, the darkest color represents a different numeric amount in each series. That defeats cross-row comparison. Choose a shared band width and number of bands for all rows being compared, and decide how out-of-range values are signaled. Clipping an extreme silently is worse than showing an overflow marker and its numeric value. Extrema-preserving reduction helps keep short-lived spikes when a long series must be downsampled before folding.

Use compactness only when it helps

A horizon chart is suited to scanning many similarly scaled time series for timing and magnitude patterns. It is weak for exact readout, unfamiliar audiences and small numbers of series, where an ordinary line chart is easier. Keep a linked detail view or accessible table with timestamp, original value, baseline, signed deviation and band encoding. Small multiples are the natural comparison when there is enough vertical space. Document the folding rule in the export so future renders preserve the same visual thresholds.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def horizon_bands(value: float, baseline: float,
                  band_width: float, band_count: int
                 ) -> tuple[str, list[float], bool]:
    if not all(isfinite(number) for number in (value, baseline, band_width)):
        raise ValueError("values must be finite")
    if band_width <= 0 or not isinstance(band_count, int) or band_count < 1:
        raise ValueError("positive band width and count required")
    delta = value - baseline
    remaining = abs(delta)
    heights = []
    for _ in range(band_count):
        height = min(remaining, band_width)
        heights.append(height)
        remaining -= height
    sign = "above" if delta > 0 else "below" if delta < 0 else "at"
    return sign, heights, remaining > 0

assert horizon_bands(87, 47, 20, 3) == ("above", [20, 20, 0], False)
assert horizon_bands(18, 47, 20, 2) == ("below", [20, 9], False)
assert horizon_bands(130, 47, 20, 3)[2] is True

Performance and operating cost

Encoding N observations with B bands takes O(NB) time and O(NB) output space when every band height is retained. The overflow flag prevents silent saturation but the rendering layer must draw a visible marker and numeric value. This function returns a sign and positive band heights; the renderer chooses color and clipping. Do not compare rows using different baselines or band widths unless the chart explicitly separates those views.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading folded height as the full original value.
  • Changing band width from row to row while reusing one color key.
  • Letting values above the maximum band range saturate without an overflow label.
  • Encoding missing as a zero deviation from baseline.

Validation drill

Display 59 equipment series around a shared service threshold. Check the band key against five exact values, mark overflows and offer a full-height line chart for one selected machine.

  • Small multiples: compare groups with honest scales and facet order

title: Animated charts: do not let motion invent data
summary: Keep record IDs, scales and frame provenance stable; offer pause and a static path through the same observations.
body:
Keep record IDs, scales and frame provenance stable; offer pause and a static path through the same observations.

Frames are data snapshots

An animated chart displays a sequence of observations, not a continuous measurement just because movement looks continuous. Store the date, source revision, eligibility rule and unit for every frame. When data exist only at two dates, intermediate positions are visual interpolation and must not be described as observed measurements. A bar that grows from 47 to 81 may imply smooth change even if the underlying quantity jumped at one import. Time-series completeness should determine which frames can be compared and which remain provisional.

Identity must survive reordering

Use stable entity IDs across frames. A ranked bar animation may reorder entities; if color or label is assigned by array position, it can appear that one entity changes into another. Match records by ID, separate newly entering and exiting entities, and never fill a missing measurement with zero unless zero is a real observation. Rank movement charts are often better as a static alternative when the main question is who changed position. Keep the selection anchored to ID if a user pauses halfway through a transition.

Lock the scale or disclose change

An axis that rescales independently at every frame can make a flat series appear to surge or a large decline look minor. Fix a domain across the full sequence when the comparison is meant to be quantitative. If an extreme new value requires a domain change, pause, label the change and provide the numeric context. Axis integrity applies to every frame, and extrema checks must run before the domain is chosen. Keep category colors, units and legend order stable too.

Motion is optional

Provide play, pause, next-frame and previous-frame controls that work with a keyboard. Do not trap focus on the chart. Respect reduced-motion preference and offer a static small-multiple view or data table that carries the same observations. A paused live feed should indicate whether resuming continues from the pause point or jumps to the latest state. Keyboard and table contracts keep the analysis available without timed interaction. Export frame ID, timestamp, scale domain and source record IDs so a particular visual state can be cited and reproduced.

Worked contract

function pairedFrameValues(previousFrame, nextFrame) {
  const previous = new Map(previousFrame.map(record => [record.id, record.value]));
  const next = new Map(nextFrame.map(record => [record.id, record.value]));
  if (previous.size !== previousFrame.length || next.size !== nextFrame.length) {
    throw new Error("each frame needs unique record IDs");
  }
  const paired = [];
  for (const [id, earlierValue] of previous) {
    if (next.has(id)) {
      const laterValue = next.get(id);
      if (!Number.isFinite(earlierValue) || !Number.isFinite(laterValue)) {
        throw new Error("frame values must be finite");
      }
      paired.push({id, earlierValue, laterValue});
    }
  }
  return paired;
}

const pairedDepots = pairedFrameValues(
  [{id: "north-47", value: 47}, {id: "south-59", value: 59}],
  [{id: "south-59", value: 81}, {id: "north-47", value: 52}],
);
if (pairedDepots[0].id !== "north-47" || pairedDepots[0].laterValue !== 52) {
  throw new Error("records must match by identity, not array position");
}

Performance and operating cost

Building two ID maps and pairing N previous records with M next records takes O(N+M) time and space. This code deliberately omits entering and exiting entities from interpolation; the view should represent them with explicit entry or exit states, not fabricate an earlier zero. A full animation also needs frame controls, reduced-motion handling, stable scales and a static equivalent. The pairing function is the data boundary that prevents position-based identity errors.

Common Mistakes

  • Presenting interpolated in-between positions as measured observations.
  • Matching reordered rows by array index so entities switch labels or colors.
  • Auto-scaling every frame while inviting quantitative comparison.
  • Autoplaying without a working pause and static way to inspect the data.

Validation drill

Animate 47 weekly depot snapshots. Lock the quantity scale, audit entry and exit states, pause on a chosen week and confirm the static table reports the same IDs and values.

  • Bump charts: show rank movement without losing ties or entrants
  • Axis scales, baselines and labels: prevent a correct number from telling a false story
  • Interactive charts: make selection work without a pointer

title: Data visualization
summary: Choose charts from the question, unit, denominator, and uncertainty the reader needs to judge.
body:
Choose charts from the question, unit, denominator, and uncertainty the reader needs to judge.

Where to begin

Start with the decision a reader must make. Then choose an encoding that preserves the relevant comparison, define the aggregation grain, and check scale, distribution, small samples, accessibility, and dashboard provenance. The linked project turns those choices into a reviewable operations display.

Read the track

  • Data Visualization Tutorial

  • Aggregation grain and denominator: make every plotted mark auditable
  • Axis scales, baselines and labels: prevent a correct number from telling a false story
  • Distribution plots: keep the tail, missing values and bin policy visible

Choose the right method

A chart with many filters can become expensive to compute and hard to interpret. Pre-aggregate only at a grain that preserves the intended question, and state when a denominator or sample size changes under a filter.

Common Mistakes

Do not truncate an axis without making the effect visible. Color alone must not carry status, and a tidy dashboard does not prove that its source query is correct.

title: Asymmetric error bars: tell readers what each endpoint means
summary: Carry lower and upper endpoints with every estimate, and never relabel arbitrary spread as uncertainty.
body:
Carry lower and upper endpoints with every estimate, and never relabel arbitrary spread as uncertainty.

The interval needs a type

An error bar may encode a standard deviation, a confidence interval, a prediction interval, an instrument tolerance or a minimum-to-maximum range. These answer different questions. Put the interval type, level where applicable, method and sample size in the chart caption. Uncertainty displays explain why a narrow-looking interval does not automatically mean a precise individual prediction. A bar without that contract invites the reader to supply the wrong interpretation. If the calculation is model-based, identify the population and conditions under which it applies.

Keep the endpoints, not just a radius

Some intervals are asymmetric around the estimate, especially near natural boundaries or after a nonlinear transform. Export estimate, lower and upper as three separate numbers. A renderer may ask for downward and upward distances, which can be derived from those endpoints without losing meaning. An estimate outside its own stated interval is a data error for many common interval definitions and should be stopped or explained. Forecast fan charts make this distinction even more important because uncertainty often widens with horizon.

Draw limits honestly

If an endpoint falls beyond the plotted axis, do not clip it silently. Extend the axis, use a visible arrow with the endpoint value, or choose another layout. A log axis cannot display zero or negative endpoints; transforming the point and interval requires the same transformation applied to both, with the method stated. Log and symmetric-log scales are not cosmetic switches. The chart should show whether a bound is physical, statistical or merely the display edge.

Compare groups without overclaiming

Overlap of two intervals is not a general significance test, and non-overlap is not the only way to establish a difference. If the decision concerns the difference between groups, estimate and plot that difference with its own interval. Signed differences put zero at the relevant comparison point. Check whether the same subjects appear in both groups; paired data require a paired calculation. For accessible reading, list each estimate and its endpoints in text, with units and the interval definition repeated where the chart may be shared alone.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def errorbar_distances(rows: list[tuple[str, float, float, float]]
                       ) -> list[tuple[str, float, float, float]]:
    names = [name for name, _, _, _ in rows]
    if len(names) != len(set(names)) or any(not name for name in names):
        raise ValueError("estimate labels must be unique and nonempty")
    output = []
    for name, estimate, lower, upper in rows:
        if not all(isfinite(value) for value in (estimate, lower, upper)):
            raise ValueError("estimate and bounds must be finite")
        if not lower <= estimate <= upper:
            raise ValueError("estimate must lie within its interval")
        output.append((name, estimate, estimate - lower, upper - estimate))
    return output

service_intervals = errorbar_distances([
    ("priority queue", 81, 59, 113),
    ("standard queue", 97, 83, 149),
])
assert service_intervals == [
    ("priority queue", 81, 22, 32),
    ("standard queue", 97, 14, 52),
]

Performance and operating cost

Preparing N intervals takes O(N) time and O(N) output space. The code validates geometry but cannot establish that endpoints were calculated with the right statistical method. Keep the original endpoints and method metadata even if the chart library wants only positive distances. Avoid computing an interval from a small sample with an unverified shortcut just because the renderer accepts two numbers.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling a range or standard deviation a confidence interval.
  • Forcing asymmetric endpoints into equal visual arms.
  • Clipping a bound at the axis edge without a marker or label.
  • Inferring a group-difference test only from overlap of separate intervals.

Validation drill

Show 59 response-time estimates with asymmetric intervals. Identify five bounds outside the current axis and revise the view without hiding those endpoints.

title: Uncertainty on charts: show denominators and intervals beside estimates
summary: A plotted estimate is not a population fact; its uncertainty and sample unit affect how strongly a visual difference can be read.
body:
A plotted estimate is not a population fact; its uncertainty and sample unit affect how strongly a visual difference can be read.

Show the independent count

Two channels can both report a 75 percent completion rate, yet one may have 12 receipts and another 12,000. Put eligible counts near marks or in an accessible companion table. If customers submit repeated receipts, the independent count may be customers rather than rows. Cluster resampling keeps those observations together.

Choose an interval contract

Specify the estimator, interval construction, confidence level and sampling unit. Error bars from an independent-row formula are misleading when assignments or outcomes cluster by reviewer. A confidence interval describes a repeated-sampling procedure; it is not a probability distribution over the displayed fixed rate. Coverage requires a valid observation process.

Separate overlap from decision

Overlapping intervals do not by themselves establish that a difference is absent, and nonoverlap is not a universal experiment test. If the task is to compare channels, calculate and display an interval for the difference under the study design. Pair this with practical limits: a two-point change may matter only above a declared volume or cost threshold.

Handle thin groups

A filter may leave one receipt or none. Use a visible “insufficient data” state rather than a narrow-looking point with absent error bars. Check that each interval is within the metric domain and that chart tooling does not clip it without notice. Keep the raw numerator and denominator available for audit.

Implementation

def interval_mark(point_rate, lower_rate, upper_rate, eligible_count):
    if eligible_count < 2:
        return {"state": "insufficient_data", "eligible_count": eligible_count}
    if not 0 <= lower_rate <= point_rate <= upper_rate <= 1:
        raise ValueError("invalid rate interval")
    return {"state": "measured", "point": point_rate,
            "lower": lower_rate, "upper": upper_rate, "eligible_count": eligible_count}

Performance and operating cost

Formatting M intervals is O(M) time and space. Interval estimation may be much more expensive, especially when resampling clusters; calculate it in a versioned data job and render the stored estimate with its construction metadata.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not draw error bars without naming their meaning.
  • Do not use receipt count as the independent sample size when customers repeat.
  • Do not interpret overlapping intervals as a complete test of a difference.

title: Correlation heatmaps: show pairwise coverage before interpreting color
summary: Keep a correlation matrix honest about missing pairs, redundant cells and feature order.
body:
Keep a correlation matrix honest about missing pairs, redundant cells and feature order.

The matrix has more than coefficients

A correlation cell describes observations shared by two variables. With missing fields, one cell may use 810 records and another 47; identical color saturation hides that difference. Carry a second matrix of pairwise counts and expose it in labels, tooltips or a companion table. A blank pair means insufficient shared records or an undefined statistic, not zero association. Missing-cell rules distinguish these states. Record which rows passed eligibility filters before calculating either matrix.

Choose a missing-data contract

Pairwise deletion uses every available pair but can give each cell a different population. Complete-case deletion holds one population constant but may discard most records and change who remains. State the choice and counts. A constant column has zero variance and no Pearson correlation; mark it undefined. Do not fill its cell with zero merely to complete a square. Dataset grain and join checks should precede calculation so duplicated rows do not inflate confidence.

Order features for the reading task

Alphabetical order is stable and auditable. A domain order groups related measures. Data-driven clustering can reveal blocks, but the clustering method and input matrix become part of the result; changing order between periods makes comparison harder. Fix order for side-by-side charts, or record the exact order for each export. Show a legend centered on zero with identical limits in every panel. Scale integrity prevents a weak coefficient from receiving the same shade as a strong one elsewhere.

Do not infer a mechanism

A large coefficient can arise from shared time trends, repeated entities, selection or a third variable. The matrix is a screen for questions, not proof that changing one field changes another. Confirm striking cells with paired scatter plots, units and source counts; outliers can dominate a linear coefficient. Avoid painting both triangles when space is tight, since the duplicate area adds no information. Dense scatter views help inspect what the matrix compressed. Describe the population and time range beside every matrix.

Worked contract

from math import sqrt

def pearson_pair(records: list[dict[str, float | None]],
                 left: str, right: str) -> tuple[float | None, int]:
    pairs = [(record[left], record[right]) for record in records
             if record.get(left) is not None and record.get(right) is not None]
    count = len(pairs)
    if count < 2:
        return None, count
    left_mean = sum(value[0] for value in pairs) / count
    right_mean = sum(value[1] for value in pairs) / count
    cross = sum((x - left_mean) * (y - right_mean) for x, y in pairs)
    left_square = sum((x - left_mean) ** 2 for x, _ in pairs)
    right_square = sum((y - right_mean) ** 2 for _, y in pairs)
    if not left_square or not right_square:
        return None, count
    return cross / sqrt(left_square * right_square), count

shipments = [{"distance": 47, "cost": 81},
             {"distance": 59, "cost": 97},
             {"distance": 71, "cost": 113},
             {"distance": 83, "cost": None}]
coefficient, paired_count = pearson_pair(shipments, "distance", "cost")
assert round(coefficient, 12) == 1 and paired_count == 3

Performance and operating cost

For P fields and N rows, a direct full matrix performs O(P²N) pair work and stores O(P²) coefficients and counts. Columnar execution can lower constant costs, but pairwise coverage still needs explicit accounting. The example returns undefined for insufficient pairs or constant values and does not provide a significance test. A precise coefficient on three shared rows is weak evidence for a broad population claim.

Common Mistakes

  • Showing a coefficient without its pairwise record count.
  • Coloring undefined correlations as zero.
  • Changing row order across comparison periods without notice.
  • Treating a strong correlation as a causal intervention result.

Validation drill

Build a five-field matrix where one field appears in only 47 of 810 records. Show the count matrix beside the coefficient matrix, then compare pairwise and complete-case populations.

title: Regression overlays: separate fitted trend from individual spread
summary: Fit on a declared population, show the data behind the line, and keep confidence and prediction bands distinct.
body:
Fit on a declared population, show the data behind the line, and keep confidence and prediction bands distinct.

Define the fit population

A line on a scatterplot is a model output, not a property of the pixels. State which rows entered the fit, the x and y units, the time window and exclusions. If the visible chart filters to one region while the line is still fitted across all regions, label that difference or refit intentionally. A pooled line can hide opposing group trends. Plot groups separately before deciding whether a shared slope is defensible. Overplotting and sampling can make a line look better supported than the visible points imply.

Do not mix two kinds of band

A confidence band for the conditional mean describes uncertainty in the estimated average curve under the model. A prediction band for a new observation includes individual variation and is normally wider. Label the band type, level and fitting method; never call an arbitrary shaded region a confidence interval. Interval endpoints should be retained in the exported data. A narrow mean band does not promise that the next delivery will land near the line.

Check influential points and model shape

One distant x value may pull a straight line through a cloud that otherwise has little trend. Inspect residuals and report the fit's valid x range. If the relationship bends, a straight line can be a poor summary even when it is easy to draw. Do not extend the overlay far beyond observed x values unless extrapolation is the explicit task and its uncertainty is shown. Q–Q diagnostics can reveal distribution departures in residuals but do not repair confounding or nonlinearity.

Keep explanation separate from causation

A rising line means the plotted variables co-vary in the selected records. It does not establish that changing x will change y. Annotate outages, policy changes or cohorts where they matter, but do not turn temporal coincidence into a mechanism. Event annotations have the same limit. Publish the coefficients and row count alongside the plot, and offer a table of fitted values if the chart is interactive. A model revision should change its version in the export so the old and new lines can be reproduced.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def fit_straight_line(points: list[tuple[float, float]]) -> tuple[float, float]:
    if len(points) < 3 or any(not (isfinite(x) and isfinite(y))
                              for x, y in points):
        raise ValueError("at least three finite pairs required")
    mean_x = sum(x for x, _ in points) / len(points)
    mean_y = sum(y for _, y in points) / len(points)
    xx = sum((x - mean_x) ** 2 for x, _ in points)
    if xx == 0:
        raise ValueError("x values need variation")
    slope = sum((x - mean_x) * (y - mean_y) for x, y in points) / xx
    return mean_y - slope * mean_x, slope

dispatch_records = [(2, 47), (3, 59), (4, 71), (5, 83)]
intercept, slope = fit_straight_line(dispatch_records)
assert (intercept, slope) == (23.0, 12.0)
assert intercept + slope * 6 == 95.0

Performance and operating cost

Computing a simple least-squares line takes O(N) time and O(1) extra space for N pairs. The code deliberately does not calculate uncertainty bands: those require a named model, assumptions, residual variance and an interval method. It is only a descriptive fit; the four exact points are a code check, not evidence of predictive accuracy. Keep the raw rows or an auditable snapshot when shipping a chart with a fitted overlay.

Common Mistakes

  • Fitting on all rows while displaying only a filtered subset without saying so.
  • Calling a mean-confidence band a prediction interval for the next record.
  • Extrapolating a straight line beyond observed x values as though support were unchanged.
  • Interpreting an association line as proof of a causal effect.

Validation drill

Fit dispatch delay against queue depth for 188 records. Compare pooled and depot-specific slopes, identify the most influential record, and label any uncertainty band with its exact meaning.

title: Stacked bars: separate composition from volume and preserve denominators
summary: Use absolute and normalized stacks for different questions, and retain every segment count.
body:
Use absolute and normalized stacks for different questions, and retain every segment count.

A stack has two possible questions

An absolute stacked bar shows a total and its parts in the same unit. A normalized bar forces every total to one and shows the mix instead. These are not interchangeable. If depot A closes 47 of 81 requests while depot B closes 470 of 810, both have the same closed share, but the latter carries ten times the workload. Place total and share in adjacent views when both matter. Define the denominator before calculating either bar. The title should say whether the horizontal extent means requests or a fraction of eligible requests.

Keep categories stable

Assign each status one color and one position across periods. If a status disappears, retain its zero-valued place in the data contract rather than shifting every later segment. The unanchored middle segments in a stack are difficult to compare precisely; when one category is the focus, use a grouped bar or a separate trend. Sort bars by a declared metric, such as eligible volume, and keep that order fixed across comparison panels. Facet ordering follows the same rule.

Handle absent and ineligible records

A missing status is not necessarily a measured zero. If the warehouse omits unresolved requests, a normalized stack can show an apparently perfect closure rate even as the unobserved group grows. Reconcile segment counts to the cohort total, expose an unknown state, and reserve a separate no-exposure state when the denominator is zero. A percentage bar for zero eligible requests has no defined composition. Missing-state display should use a label or pattern in addition to color.

Audit every filter

When a dashboard filters by region or week, recompute each segment count from the selected cohort and normalize only after filtering. Do not average prior percentages. Tooltips and exports should include segment count, denominator and percentage; rounded shares may sum to 99.9 or 100.1, which is a display effect rather than a data error. Linked selections must update totals and segments together. Test one-bar, zero-cohort and category-absent states before release.

Worked contract

def composition_by_depot(
    counts: dict[str, dict[str, int]], statuses: tuple[str, ...]
) -> dict[str, dict[str, tuple[int, float | None]]]:
    if len(set(statuses)) != len(statuses) or not statuses:
        raise ValueError("statuses must be unique and nonempty")
    result = {}
    for depot, segments in counts.items():
        if set(segments) - set(statuses) or any(value < 0 for value in segments.values()):
            raise ValueError("unknown status or negative count")
        total = sum(segments.values())
        result[depot] = {
            status: (segments.get(status, 0),
                     segments.get(status, 0) / total if total else None)
            for status in statuses
        }
    return result

mix = composition_by_depot(
    {"north": {"closed": 47, "pending": 34},
     "south": {"closed": 470, "pending": 340}},
    ("closed", "pending", "unknown"))
assert mix["north"]["closed"] == (47, 47 / 81)
assert mix["south"]["closed"] == (470, 470 / 810)
assert mix["north"]["unknown"] == (0, 0.0)

Performance and operating cost

For D depots, S declared statuses and M supplied segment values, validation and construction take O(M + DS) expected time and O(DS) output space. Reusing a prebuilt status set removes repeated set construction in a larger implementation. Rendering a normalized bar still needs the absolute counts for labels and audit. The example treats an absent segment as observed zero only under the stated complete-status contract; without that contract, an absent segment must be marked unknown.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading equal-width normalized bars as equal workloads.
  • Dropping unresolved statuses before calculating shares.
  • Changing stack order between weeks and implying a category moved.
  • Averaging percentages instead of adding segment counts first.

Validation drill

Prepare 13 weekly depot bars with different cohort sizes. Show absolute and normalized versions, then remove one status record from a source extract and verify reconciliation fails rather than silently improving a percentage.

title: Waterfall charts: reconcile every step to the closing total
summary: Model changes as signed contributions, and keep subtotals distinct from new contributions.
body:
Model changes as signed contributions, and keep subtotals distinct from new contributions.

A bridge is an equation

A waterfall begins with an opening amount, applies signed changes in a declared order, and ends with a closing amount. Every floating bar implies a cumulative level before and after its step. The diagram is useful when the question is why a total changed, but the numbers must reconcile exactly. An unexplained residual should be shown as a named residual, not hidden in the last bar. The aggregation grain must stay stable: summing transaction-level changes and mixing them with account-level balances can double count.

Separate a subtotal from a change

A subtotal displays the running balance at a checkpoint; it does not add to that balance again. A renderer may call an item relative, absolute or total, but the source data should declare its semantic role independently of the library. Recalculate every subtotal from the opening amount and preceding changes. If a reported checkpoint disagrees, stop the publication pipeline or show the discrepancy explicitly. The export contract should keep item role, signed amount, running level and source period.

Choose order without inventing causality

Steps may be ordered by business process, chronology or contribution magnitude. A magnitude order helps show large drivers but can imply a process order that never occurred; label it as a decomposition rather than an event timeline. If two drivers overlap, their estimated contributions may not be independently additive. State the allocation rule before drawing. Annotations and causal claims require more evidence than a visually convenient bridge. For an exact ledger, preserve source transaction IDs or reconciliation batches.

Read signed values and scale

A decrease may be good or bad depending on the metric. Use text and bar direction as well as color. A zero step should remain in the export but can be collapsed in a crowded display if the omission is stated. If the starting balance is negative, make zero visible and verify connectors still show the true running level. Signed comparison charts are better when the task is ranking independent gaps rather than explaining one total. Test refunds, reversals, missing steps and rounding before release.

Worked contract

from decimal import Decimal

def reconcile_bridge(opening: Decimal,
                     steps: list[tuple[str, Decimal]],
                     expected_close: Decimal) -> list[tuple[str, Decimal]]:
    if len({name for name, _ in steps}) != len(steps):
        raise ValueError("step names must be unique")
    running = opening
    levels = [("opening", running)]
    for name, change in steps:
        running += change
        levels.append((name, running))
    if running != expected_close:
        raise ValueError("bridge does not reconcile")
    return levels

bridge = reconcile_bridge(
    Decimal("810.00"),
    [("new contracts", Decimal("147.00")),
     ("returns", Decimal("-59.00")),
     ("credits", Decimal("-81.00"))],
    Decimal("817.00"))
assert bridge[-1] == ("credits", Decimal("817.00"))

Performance and operating cost

For S changes, reconciliation is O(S) time and O(S) output space. The currency example uses Decimal so binary floating-point rounding does not create a false residual. The code validates the exact closing balance but does not check whether step categories overlap or whether source ledger rows were omitted; those are upstream accounting controls. A large waterfall often needs grouped minor steps, with an auditable rollup behind the group.

Common Mistakes

  • Adding a subtotal as though it were another contribution.
  • Forcing the final bar to the reported close despite a residual.
  • Mixing time periods or grains in one bridge.
  • Using color alone to identify increase and decrease.

Validation drill

Explain a move from 810 to 817 units with three signed steps. Then remove the credit step and verify reconciliation fails. Add a subtotal after returns without changing the closing amount.

title: Axis scales, baselines and labels: prevent a correct number from telling a false story
summary: Axis choices change visual distance, so the scale must match the comparison and be disclosed wherever it changes interpretation.
body:
Axis choices change visual distance, so the scale must match the comparison and be disclosed wherever it changes interpretation.

Use a meaningful baseline

Bar length is read against its baseline. Starting a bar axis at 0.71 can make two completion rates of 0.74 and 0.77 look several times apart. Use zero for ordinary bar lengths and show exact values when a small difference matters. A line chart may use a narrower range to show variation, but the displayed bounds and units must remain obvious.

Inspect transformations

A logarithmic axis can reveal values across orders of magnitude, but equal screen distances then represent equal ratios rather than equal differences. Zero and negative values need an explicit treatment. Never switch an axis to logarithmic merely to fit an outlier, and never compare a linear-panel slope with a log-panel slope as though they share meaning.

Keep category order honest

Sort categories by a documented metric or a stable domain order. If the order changes at each refresh, motion can look like a performance shift when values are steady. Labels should state percent versus percentage points; moving from 74 to 77 percent is a three-point change, not a three-percent relative change. The chart question decides which comparison is primary.

Test presentation rules

Prepare two rates, 0.74 and 0.77, and verify both bars share zero. Then format them as 74.0% and 77.0%. If a narrow view clips labels, retain an accessible text table. Recheck after filtering because an automatic axis may silently rescale and change the apparent difference.

Implementation

def percentage_point_change(previous_rate, current_rate):
    if not all(0 <= rate <= 1 for rate in (previous_rate, current_rate)):
        raise ValueError("rates must be between zero and one")
    return (current_rate - previous_rate) * 100

change_points = percentage_point_change(0.74, 0.77)

Performance and operating cost

Scale formatting is O(M) for M plotted marks. The larger cost is review: test every filter state that changes axis bounds, zero visibility or label collisions. Cache formatted labels only when underlying rate and unit versions match.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not truncate a bar axis without making the baseline explicit.
  • Do not label a percentage-point movement as a relative percent.
  • Do not hide nonpositive observations when using a logarithmic scale.

title: Small multiples: compare groups with honest scales and facet order
summary: Repeat one chart grammar across groups, then choose shared or local axes according to the intended comparison.
body:
Repeat one chart grammar across groups, then choose shared or local axes according to the intended comparison.

A facet is a repeated measurement frame

Small multiples split the same visual grammar into panels, one per group. They reduce line crossings and legend lookup when a single plot has too many series. The gain depends on consistency: each panel should use the same measure, time window, mark type and aggregation rule. A panel for customer tickets and a panel for revenue do not become comparable simply because they share a grid. Declare the measure before arranging panels. Keep a visible label on each panel; color alone is insufficient.

Shared scales answer magnitude questions

If the reader needs to know which depot has the largest delay, a shared y-domain lets equal heights mean equal values. Local y-domains can make a low-volume depot's variation legible, but a steep line then no longer means a larger absolute change. If independent domains are necessary, print the local minimum and maximum in every panel and avoid a headline about cross-panel magnitude. Axis integrity applies to every facet. For percentages, a fixed zero-to-one domain is often an honest baseline; for residuals around zero, a symmetric domain may expose sign and spread better.

Keep the time window and missingness aligned

Shared x-axes help readers distinguish a simultaneous event from a panel-specific shift. A region with no observations on Wednesday should show a gap, not compress its calendar so Thursday occupies Wednesday's position. When groups enter the system at different times, an aligned calendar makes the unequal exposure visible. Time-series gap rules should be applied before faceting. If panels use different time windows by design, label them prominently and avoid visual comparison of positions.

Order panels for the task

Alphabetical order is stable but often unhelpful when inspecting performance. Sorting by a predeclared baseline or current value can put high-risk groups first; automatic resorting on every hover makes the layout hard to track. Record the sort key and freeze it for an analysis session. Do not omit small groups without stating a threshold and the number omitted. Small-sample uncertainty often explains why an apparently extreme panel should receive inspection rather than a confident ranking.

Budget the screen

Thirty tiny panels may be technically complete yet unreadable on a phone. Allow searching or paging through stable groups while keeping the same scale contract. A summary panel can show the total or reference band, but it must follow the same population rules. Test keyboard order and screen-reader panel labels. If each facet needs a unique tooltip, interaction cost grows with the number of panels; prioritize a simple data table for exact values. A chart grid should make comparisons easier, not force the reader to memorize dozens of legends.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def facet_domains(series: dict[str, list[float]],
                  shared: bool) -> dict[str, tuple[float, float]]:
    if not series or any(not values for values in series.values()):
        raise ValueError("each facet needs observed values")
    if any(not isfinite(value) for values in series.values() for value in values):
        raise ValueError("non-finite plotted value")
    if shared:
        values = [value for group in series.values() for value in group]
        domain = (min(values), max(values))
        return {name: domain for name in series}
    return {name: (min(values), max(values)) for name, values in series.items()}

depot_delays = {"north": [18, 47], "south": [3, 8]}
assert facet_domains(depot_delays, True)["south"] == (3, 47)
assert facet_domains(depot_delays, False)["south"] == (3, 8)

Performance and operating cost

For N values across G groups, scanning domains takes O(N + G) time. The shared branch stores an extra O(N) flattened list for clarity; a streaming minimum and maximum reduce that auxiliary memory to O(1), while the returned G domains still need O(G) space. Rendering cost scales with both the number of panels and marks. A UI that rerenders every facet after each filter may become slow even when the domain calculation is cheap; memoize by the complete filter and data-version key only when measurements justify it.

Common Mistakes

  • Using independent y-domains while claiming one group has the larger magnitude.
  • Dropping missing dates and shifting one panel's x positions relative to the rest.
  • Reordering facets during interaction without labeling the sort key.
  • Suppressing tiny cohorts without reporting how many groups were hidden.

Validation drill

Facet five depot delay series on one weekly calendar. Produce a shared-scale view for absolute comparison and a labeled independent-scale view for within-depot variation; write down which conclusions differ.

title: Bump charts: show rank movement without losing ties or entrants
summary: Declare the ranking metric, tie policy and eligible entities for each period before connecting positions.
body:
Declare the ranking metric, tie policy and eligible entities for each period before connecting positions.

Rank is an ordering, not a magnitude

A bump chart connects an entity's ranks across periods. A move from third to first may reflect a tiny absolute difference or a major change; the line does not tell you which. Name the ranked measure and link to values behind each position. Paired-change charts work better when the actual size of change matters. If a new entity enters the cohort, existing ranks can fall without their own measurements changing. Display entrants and exits as membership events rather than implying deterioration.

Ties need a written rule

Equal measurements can share a rank, be assigned adjacent ranks by a secondary key, or be shown in a tied band. These choices produce different line paths. Competition ranking gives equal values the same rank and skips the next position; dense ranking does not skip. Neither should be selected by accident inside a plotting library. Preserve raw values and the chosen tie rule in the export. Reproducible chart exports also need source period and eligibility criteria. Test ties at both top and bottom before publishing.

Hold the cohort question steady

A panel can rank the same fixed set of entities every period or rank whoever was eligible at the time. The first view tracks a stable cohort; the second reflects changing membership. State which one readers see. If a missing measurement removes an entity from one period, show a line break or missing marker rather than assigning last place. Provisional periods and data gaps are especially easy to hide in a rank-only display. Mark a period as provisional when its numerator or denominator can still change.

Limit crossings and preserve access

Many crossing lines defeat tracing. Highlight a small set chosen by a documented rule, fade the remainder and let the reader search by entity ID. A table with period, rank, value and membership status is essential, because color-only line identity and hover-only labels fail on touch and assistive technology. Text alternatives should call out the biggest rank rise, biggest fall, ties and entrants. Do not claim a trend from two ranks alone; a third period or actual values may tell a different story.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def competition_ranks(scores: dict[str, float]) -> dict[str, int]:
    if any(not entity for entity in scores):
        raise ValueError("entity IDs must be nonempty")
    if any(not isfinite(value) for value in scores.values()):
        raise ValueError("scores must be finite")
    ordered = sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda item: (-item[1], item[0]))
    ranks = {}
    prior_score = None
    current_rank = 0
    for position, (entity, score) in enumerate(ordered, start=1):
        if prior_score is None or score != prior_score:
            current_rank = position
        ranks[entity] = current_rank
        prior_score = score
    return ranks

week_47 = competition_ranks({"north": 81, "south": 81,
                             "west": 59, "east": 47})
assert week_47 == {"north": 1, "south": 1, "west": 3, "east": 4}

Performance and operating cost

Ranking N entities costs O(N log N) time and O(N) output space per period; connecting P periods takes O(PN) output storage for a fixed cohort. The code uses higher-score-first competition ranks and stable ID ordering only for reproducible output. It does not fill absent entities. Before rendering, validate that every period uses the same score definition and disclose whether the eligible set is fixed or variable.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading a one-place rise as a fixed-size improvement.
  • Allowing a chart library to break ties arbitrarily.
  • Assigning missing entities last place.
  • Comparing periods with changing eligibility without labeling entrants and exits.

Validation drill

Rank 47 service depots over six weeks with two ties and one new entrant. Reconcile every rank to its score and show how the entrant changes the apparent position of unchanged depots.

title: Interactive charts: make selection work without a pointer
summary: Treat focus, selection and the data table as part of the chart's public interface.
body:
Treat focus, selection and the data table as part of the chart's public interface.

Hover is not access

A tooltip visible only on pointer hover excludes keyboard and many touch users. Give each interactive mark a reachable focus target, a meaningful accessible name and the same detail on focus as on hover. Arrow keys can move within a series, while Home and End can jump to its bounds; publish the key rules next to the chart. Keep a visible focus indicator. Color and text alternatives cover the static layer, but a chart with filters and selections also needs an interaction contract.

Separate focus from selection

Focus says where keyboard input will act. Selection says which records are included in the current analysis. Do not silently change the filter merely because focus moved to another point. If Enter selects a point, announce the new selection and update the related table or summary. A selected range should survive a resize and a redraw by stable record IDs rather than pixel coordinates. Linked filters and cohort state should make the selected population and denominator visible across all charts.

Avoid a thousand tab stops

Putting every mark in the page's normal Tab sequence can make a dense chart unusable. A single chart entry point followed by arrow-key movement may be better, provided the active point's name and value are exposed, the user can exit with Tab, and the navigation order is predictable. Do not trap focus inside the plot. For large series, offer direct search, a bounded table, or a downloadable data file so a user does not have to press an arrow 4,700 times. Large-series reduction must preserve access to underlying records when visual points are aggregated.

The table is a first-class view

An accessible data table should use the same filters, units, missing-value markers and ordering as the chart. If the chart displays a sampled or binned series, identify that fact and provide a route to full records when appropriate. Do not generate a table from SVG positions; derive both views from one data model. Export provenance should include the selection, filter and sort state so a shared screenshot and a CSV tell the same story. Test with only a keyboard, at narrow width, and with zoom before publication.

Worked contract

function nextChartPoint(currentIndex, pointCount, key) {
  if (!Number.isInteger(pointCount) || pointCount < 1 ||
      !Number.isInteger(currentIndex) || currentIndex < 0 ||
      currentIndex >= pointCount) {
    throw new RangeError("chart point state is invalid");
  }
  if (key === "ArrowRight" || key === "ArrowDown") {
    return Math.min(currentIndex + 1, pointCount - 1);
  }
  if (key === "ArrowLeft" || key === "ArrowUp") {
    return Math.max(currentIndex - 1, 0);
  }
  if (key === "Home") return 0;
  if (key === "End") return pointCount - 1;
  return currentIndex;
}

const visibleRecordIds = ["depot-47", "depot-59", "depot-83"];
let focusedIndex = 0;
focusedIndex = nextChartPoint(focusedIndex, visibleRecordIds.length, "End");
if (visibleRecordIds[focusedIndex] !== "depot-83") {
  throw new Error("keyboard focus must follow chart order");
}
if (nextChartPoint(focusedIndex, visibleRecordIds.length, "ArrowRight") !== 2) {
  throw new Error("focus must stop at the last record");
}

Performance and operating cost

A key transition takes O(1) time and space; the displayed order and accessible table require O(N) record storage for N visible points. The pure function handles movement only. The browser component must connect it to focus, accessible names, announcement text and selection state, and must retain Tab exit. If a virtualized chart reorders records, map stable IDs to the new order before restoring focus. Treat the table as the source-aligned view, not as a decorative duplicate.

Common Mistakes

  • Making hover-only tooltip content unavailable on focus and touch.
  • Changing the selected cohort whenever a user merely moves focus.
  • Adding every dense-series mark to the Tab order with no shortcut or data table.
  • Restoring focus by pixel position after filter changes instead of stable record identity.

Validation drill

Audit a 188-point chart using only keyboard navigation. Verify focus visibility, Enter selection, Tab exit, a synchronized table and stable record identity after a filter change.
